title: Light the Way
subtitle: The Legend of Corin Ashvale
teaser: He climbed the cliffs of Varrow on a bet, and the lighthouse keeper’s daughter met him at the top with a jug of lamp oil. Then, on the last night of autumn, the sky turned green.

sections.heading: I. The Lighthouse Keeper’s Daughter
paragraphs: Corin Ashvale was nineteen the first time he climbed the cliffs of Varrow at night. He only did it because someone bet him he couldn’t.
Halfway up, a lamp swung out over the edge above him. A girl held it. In her other hand she held a jug of lamp oil, tipped right over his head.
“Give me one reason,” she said, “why I shouldn’t.”
He was clinging to wet rock by his fingertips. The only reason he could think of was the truth. “Because then I’d never find out your name.”
She laughed so hard she nearly dropped the lamp. Her name was Isra Venn, and she was the lighthouse keeper’s daughter.

Varrow was a town that lived by the sea and died by it. Storms came off the Grey Water without warning, and the lighthouse was the only thing that brought the fishing boats home. Isra had tended its lamp since she was eight, and she could read a storm the way other people read faces.
That first year, she taught him the names of clouds. Anvil-heads meant trouble. Mackerel skies meant change. Green light on the horizon meant run.

In return, he taught her what the old harbor watchman had taught him: how to hold a spear, how to plant your feet, how to throw so the whole body follows. She was terrible at it. She threw like she was apologizing to the target, and he loved her for it anyway.

By the second year, he was climbing the cliff path every evening with bread, smoked fish, and whatever wildflowers survived the salt. They’d sit on the gallery around the great lamp with their legs dangling over the edge and talk about nothing until the stars came out.
“One day I’ll build us a house,” he told her once. “Somewhere the sea can’t reach.”
“The sea reaches everywhere, Corin.”
“Then what’s the point of building anything?”

She leaned her head on his shoulder and watched the beam sweep out over the black water. “The point is you build it anyway. That’s what this whole tower is. Somebody building something the sea can’t take.”
He didn’t understand what she meant yet. He would.

sections.heading: II. The Storm With a Name
paragraphs: The sky turned green on the last night of autumn.

Isra’s father, old Maren Venn, called Corin up to the tower before the first raindrop fell. Isra was down at the docks with a hand lamp, waving the last boats in. Maren looked older than Corin had ever seen him, and he told Corin a story every keeper had sworn never to repeat.

Some storms are weather. One is not. Every few hundred years, something rises out of the deep water wearing a storm like a cloak. The old texts called it Vharos, the Tempest-Eater. It feeds on lightning, and when the lightning isn’t enough, it feeds on towns.

The lighthouse had never been built just to guide ships. It was built on top of a vault. In that vault, chained in iron and salt, lay Thunderreach: a spear forged from the first bolt of lightning that ever struck the world. It was the only weapon that had ever wounded Vharos.
“Then we use it,” Corin said.
Maren shook his head. “Flesh can’t hold it. Lightning needs somewhere to live. The spear takes a heart, a storm-blooded heart, a keeper’s heart. And it never gives it back.”
He had always meant for it to be his. He was old, he said. He’d had his life. He said it calmly, like a man describing tomorrow’s weather.
Then the storm reached the harbor, and a bolt came down through the lantern room like a fist.

Maren Venn was dead before he finished his sentence. Corin stood in the smoking wreck of the lantern room, ears ringing, and understood all at once that there was only one keeper’s heart left in Varrow.

sections.heading: III. The Price
paragraphs: He didn’t go to find her. He went down.

The vault stairs spiraled into the cliff, slick with seawater. At the bottom, in a chamber of black stone, Thunderreach hung in its chains and hummed like a struck bell. Blue-white light crawled along its shaft.
Corin broke the chains with a harbor axe. Then he wrapped his right hand around the spear.

The lightning went through him like a verdict. It seared a branching scar into his palm and threw him across the chamber. He got up and grabbed it again. And again. Each time it threw him harder. It didn’t want him. It wanted what it had been promised.
“Stop,” Isra said from the stairs. “You’ll kill yourself, and it still won’t work.”
She was soaked and shaking, and she was not surprised. That was the worst part. She had known since she was a little girl and her father first walked her down those stairs.
“No,” Corin said. “There’s another way. We run. We take a boat.”
“Where?” she asked gently. “The sea reaches everywhere. Remember?”
She came down the last steps and took his burned hand in both of hers. Above them, the whole cliff shook. They could hear the town screaming.
“You were always going to be the one who throws it,” she said. “And I was always going to be the one who lights the way. That’s what a lighthouse is for.”
He begged her. He would remember that later and never be ashamed of it. He begged her the way he had never begged anyone for anything.
She kissed him once, slowly, like they had all the time in the world. Then she laid her free hand on the spear.

There was no scream. There was no blast. The light simply went out of her the way a candle goes out, and came on in the spear instead. She was gone before she reached the floor, and he caught her anyway.
Thunderreach lay in his hand, and it didn’t burn anymore. It was warm. Exactly as warm as her hand had been a moment before.

sections.heading: IV. The Throw
paragraphs: The lamp at the top of the tower was dark for the first time in three hundred years. Out in the harbor, the fishing boats were lost in the black.
Corin climbed every one of the four hundred steps with the spear in his hand. When he reached the gallery where they used to sit with their legs over the edge, Vharos was waiting.

It filled the sky: a wall of cloud with a single pale eye at its center, ringed in lightning. Wind tore at him. Rain came sideways like thrown gravel. The storm looked at the dark lighthouse, and at the small man standing on it, and did not see a threat.
Corin raised the spear, and the tower lit up.
Not the lamp. Him. Lightning poured out of Thunderreach, down his arm, across the gallery, so bright that every boat in the harbor turned toward it and started rowing home.
He planted his feet. He let his whole body follow, the way he’d taught her.
“Light the way,” he whispered, and threw.

The spear went into the eye of the storm like a needle into a heart. For one long moment there was no sound at all. Then the sky split open from horizon to horizon, and Vharos came apart into ordinary rain.
The spear came back to his hand. It always would.
By dawn the sea was flat and silver. The town crept out into the wreckage and found him at the top of the cliff, digging. He was burying her on the spot where he’d promised to build their house.
When he was done, he didn’t put up a stone. He just sat there until the sun was all the way up, holding the spear across his knees like something asleep.

sections.heading: V. The Man Who Walks Alone
paragraphs: In the places he passes through, they call him the Stormwarden. Some call him the Lightning That Walks. Almost nobody calls him Corin anymore.

He never stays anywhere longer than a season. He hunts the things that come out of storms and the things that come out of men: raiders, drowned gods, kings who think the weak are kindling. He arrives when the sky turns green, and he leaves before anyone can thank him properly.

He is kind to children and patient with old men. He drinks alone. He has turned down more warm beds than most men are ever offered, always gently, always with the same small smile, like someone declining a gift he has no room to carry.
People assume he’s cold. He isn’t. He already has someone to come home to, and he carries her in his right hand.

Nobody has ever heard him say the spear’s name. Ask him, and he’ll look at you for a long moment and say nothing at all. But soldiers who have fought beside him swear that right before he throws, he whispers something. Three words. And the lightning always answers, like it was waiting to hear his voice.

On stormy nights he sleeps sitting up, Thunderreach across his knees, the branching scar on his palm pressed against the shaft. Sometimes the thunder rolls in a rhythm that sounds almost like laughter. Those are the nights he sleeps well.
He was never the strongest man in the world. He just carries the bravest person he ever knew, and every time he throws, she lights the way.
